rules: An id, once published, is never renamed, reused or removed. Your progress is stored against ids, so it survives every update.
Updates replace the app and its content. They never touch app/data, where your progress and your solution files live.
New quiz questions are added at the end of a topic. New exercises join an existing skill or come with a new one.
Dated material, such as the frontier papers, is added as a new snapshot beside the old one, not written over it.
Every exercise is checked before release: its reference solution must pass its tests and its starter must fail them.

changes: Lessons for every stage: nine new lessons cover Stages 1 to 8, from NumPy and backpropagation to the transformer, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, ROS 2 and federated learning. Each one lists its Build rows to tick and the book chapters to read beside it. There are 24 lessons in all.

Generative AI, as asked in 2026 interviews: Stage 9 in the Build list, four lessons, and 28 exercises on decoding, the KV cache, quantisation, speculative decoding, retrieval and its metrics, fine-tuning losses, LoRA, DPO, tool calls, agent loops, rate limits, caching, cost and streaming.
SQL: 16 queries on a small bank's tables, from filters to window functions, streaks and retention. They run in SQLite, offline, in the laptop and the browser version alike.

Statistics and experiments: 20 exercises on Bayes, intervals, tests, the bootstrap, permutation tests, A/B testing, sample size, sample ratio mismatch, multiple metrics, validation without leakage, AUC, thresholds, calibration and weight of evidence. Each was checked against SciPy and scikit-learn.

Books and repos, a new list: 262 rows from 21 books, courses and repositories, among them Hands-On Machine Learning (PyTorch edition), Raschka's two from-scratch books, Karpathy's repositories, Hands-On Large Language Models, AI Engineering, Designing Machine Learning Systems, the Hugging Face courses, Kaggle Learn, LeetCode SQL 50 and the DataTalksClub zoomcamps. Each row is placed at a stage, and every GitHub link was checked against its repository.
Mock interview rounds under Practice: a coding round, a generative AI round, an SQL screen, a statistics round and ML system design, each timed, with hints and solutions locked until the round ends.

Keeping the streak: a daily reminder you add to your calendar (Settings), a two-minute option on Today when time is short, and a warning in the evening when the streak would end at midnight. Ticks in the Books list and on lesson pages count for the streak.

Interview list: generative AI, ML system design, data science and experiments, and behavioural sections, 36 rows. Papers: 12 generative AI papers with read, implement and reproduce steps. Replays: a Kaggle Playground starter that can be repeated every month.
61 new quiz questions in two new topics, generative AI systems and A/B tests; 325 in all. 15 new skills on the Map and a new role track, data scientist for banking, fintech and product.
Whole numbers in test output now have to match exactly; numbers with a decimal point still match within a small tolerance.

QR codes, for a device that cannot send files: Settings, Your devices, Show as QR codes puts your progress on the screen as a few codes, and Scan QR codes on another device reads them with its camera, or from photos of them. Nothing to copy, send or install, so it works from an office laptop.
Each time, only what is new since the last codes is sent: a day's work is a handful of codes. Everything can still be sent at once.

Your devices, under Settings: save your progress as a file and add it on another device. Adding a file only adds what is new and never removes anything, so it works in both directions. Solved exercises, runs, quiz answers, recall notes and their schedule, ticks, focus sessions, paper notes and your solution files all travel. Send the file by Bluetooth, email, a cable or a drive; on a phone there is a button to send it straight away.

A browser version of the whole app, at https://manojhunasimarad.github.io/llm-from-zero/. Python runs inside the browser, so it works on a phone or a work laptop with nothing installed, and offline after the first visit. It can be installed from the browser like an app. Each browser keeps its own progress; Your devices brings them level. The agent and fetching papers by link stay in this laptop version.

CUDA and parallel computing, which the app did not teach before: three lessons and 14 exercises on speedup, caches, GPU kernels, MapReduce and message passing. The GPU exercises are in Python with CUDA's own names and need no graphics card; each shows the same kernel in CUDA C once solved.

A Syllabus list that follows the six core courses of the M.Tech in Computational and Data Science at NITK: what to explain from memory, what to write here, and 17 programs to run and time on a real machine in CUDA C, OpenMP, MPI and Spark.
Numerical methods: 11 exercises on roots, integrals, derivatives, interpolation, elimination, LU and iterative solvers.
Markov chains and queues: 5 exercises, from the stationary distribution and the M/M/1 queue to PageRank and the first singular vector.
From the algorithms course: quicksort, minimum spanning trees, Floyd-Warshall, and sparse and circulant matrices. 56 DSA problems in all.
71 new quiz questions: three new topics (parallel computing and CUDA, numerical methods, stochastic processes and queues) and additions to four others. 264 in all.
Seven new skills on the Map, a Parallel and GPU tab and a Numerical tab under Practice, and one more card on Today.

Recall: when you tick a video, a paper or an interview topic, or finish a lesson, the app asks for two or three lines from memory. The note comes back after a day, a week and a month, and you write again before you see it.

Quiz questions you miss come back under Recall as open questions, with no options to recognise. In practice mode the options stay hidden until you have an answer in mind; a switch under the question turns that off.

Focus: a timer that stays in the top bar, with five techniques (Pomodoro 25/5, 50/10, a 90-minute deep block, Flowtime and a five-minute start), a record of which ones you finish, and a note to yourself on where to pick up.
Read: a shelf for papers. Upload a PDF or paste a link, and the paper opens beside notes for three passes. Rows in the Papers and Frontier lists have a "Read here" link.

Your agent: an optional language model on your own GPU, through Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible server. It summarises a paper once you have written your own claim, answers questions with page numbers, quizzes you, shows what a recall attempt missed, and gives a nudge on an exercise without writing code.
Settings can look for a GPU and for Ollama and say what size of model fits. A college server can be used through an SSH tunnel.
Today leads with what is due for recall and shows your minutes of focus against a daily goal.
The Watch list is rebuilt from your own YouTube subscriptions. All 111 channels were gone through; 68 of them now have rows, placed by stage and by role topic, 147 rows in all.
Links go to the exact playlist or video, read from each channel's own pages, not to the channel.
Each section marks one row as the place to start.
Every skill page on the Map now shows the two to four series that teach that skill.
The subscribed channels without a row are named at the top of the Watch list, with the reason.
The app now chooses the next problem. Solve one without help and it offers the harder version; solve it with hints and it offers one more at the same level; get stuck and it offers a step back.
A skill map: 32 skills from Python basics to agents, with what each one needs and unlocks, coloured by how strong you are in each.
Rewrite from memory: one day, one week and one month after you solve an exercise, the app asks you to write it again on a blank page.
26 new DSA problems, covering bits, linked lists, trees, binary search trees, heaps, queues and graphs. 50 in all.
Video 70: every chapter of the stoney codes video as a checklist, with a link to the moment in the video and, for 36 of them, a version to solve here offline.
Replays: three winning competition solutions rebuilt version by version, with a box for your own score at each step.
Frontier: a dated list of trending papers on agents, robotics and efficient inference, for practising triage.
Role tracks for robotics and edge AI, LLM and agents, reinforcement learning, federated learning and MLOps, each with what its interviews ask and how ready you are on the parts this app can measure.
64 new quiz questions in five topics: complexity, MLOps, RAG and agents, federated learning, edge deployment. 193 in all.
Today shows a twelve-week activity calendar and your longest streak. Settings shows the content version and can look for PyTorch and a GPU.
A watch list of free lecture series, placed by stage.
First version: the Stage 0 Python course, 44 exercises with tests, hints and solutions, the open ML problem set, 129 quiz questions, mock exams, certificate maps and four checklists.
